Power supply, or PSU, power supply unit. It converts incoming alternating current from the wall outlet into regulated direct current at multiple voltage levels required by a computer's components. It distributes power safely to the CPU, RAM, storage devices, and peripheral components while protecting them from voltage spikes and brownouts. Power supply capacity, measured in watts, must exceed the system's peak demand to ensure stable operation.

The supply contains a transformer that steps down voltage and a rectifier that converts AC to DC, followed by filtering and regulation stages. A modern PSU outputs plus or minus three point three volts, plus or minus five volts, plus or minus twelve volts, and plus or minus twenty-four volts to different components. The twelve-volt rail typically supplies the CPU and GPU.

Standard eighty Plus certifications indicate what fraction of input power is delivered to components versus lost as heat. The certifications are Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium. Gold and higher supplies are approximately ninety percent efficient. A five hundred-watt supply means continuous rated output at full load, though peak surge capacity is higher. Undersized supplies throttle performance, while oversized supplies operate below peak efficiency.

Modern supplies have disconnectable modular cabling so users route only what they need, improving airflow and cable management. Protection circuits for overvoltage, overcurrent, and thermal shutdown safeguards prevent damage to expensive components from electrical faults. Supplies maintain a small five-volt rail even when the computer is off, powering standby features like wake-on-LAN and USB charging, making power supply the critical interface between grid AC and digital DC logic.
